situation: I was working as a frontend engineer on a financial application. The backend engineer I depended on for a key integration was based in a timezone roughly 12 hours apart from mine, which left very little overlap in our working hours. Communication was also harder than usual because of a strong accent on his side and the fact that I'm not a native English speaker myself, so quick verbal exchanges often led to misunderstandings.
task: I needed to resolve integration issues on an important feature, but the time difference meant we rarely could just hop on a call to sort things out, and when we did talk, language friction made it easy to misinterpret technical details. I had to find a way to keep the integration moving without constant real-time back-and-forth.
action: I pushed for us to write proper API documentation describing how the integration was supposed to work, so expectations were captured in writing rather than depending on verbal explanations that were easy to lose across the time zone and language gap.
result: The integration issues got resolved without needing to force overlapping hours, and the API documentation became something the wider team adopted going forward, so other developers could understand how the integration worked without needing a live conversation either.

situation: I was working as a frontend engineer on a web dashboard product that gathered knowledge base content from multiple sources — including Zendesk and other admin-entered URLs — crawled that content, and stored it in Azure AI Search and Azure Blob Storage. At one point my manager flagged that a key feature was falling behind schedule and that the team needed to catch up.
task: I was asked to take on work on this feature even though it required backend and AI/crawling knowledge I didn't have prior experience with. I needed to get up to speed quickly and deliver without slowing the team down further.
action: I didn't hesitate to take it on despite the knowledge gap. I used AI-assisted development tools to help me learn the unfamiliar stack quickly and apply it correctly. I worked on building out the crawler logic — the part of the system that crawled the source data and saved it into Azure Blob Storage and Azure AI Search.
result: I successfully got the crawled data saving correctly into Blob Storage and  Azure AI Search, and the feature shipped. Taking on that stretch work outside my usual frontend scope contributed to my being promoted to team lead afterward.

situation: I was moved from another project onto AgencyOS, a large application that handles AI agent workflows, even though I didn't have as much prior experience with this kind of system as the project required. I was assigned to a specific workflow: a Front-Airtable integration, where the system analyzes incoming messages to determine if they represent a task. If so, it posts a description to a Slack channel, where the responsible person can approve, reject, or edit it — and depending on their decision. If it is approved, a corresponding task gets created in Airtable. We had just one week to get this working.
task: When I started, the hop logic — the core branching logic that routed the workflow between steps — was broken to the point where I couldn't even get it to run. I needed to fix this and get the integration working reliably within the one-week deadline, despite limited familiarity with the codebase and the AI agent workflow patterns it used.
action: I went through extensive troubleshooting and testing to isolate and fix the broken hop logic, working through one issue after another as I uncovered them. Once it was running, to make sure the LLM-driven task-classification logic wasn't hallucinating or misclassifying messages, I built and used evaluation pipelines to systematically validate its outputs rather than just spot-checking manually.
result: Within the one-week deadline, I got the integration to a stable beta state, and it passed beta testing with good results from the client. The feature was then deployed to production.

situation: I was asked to integrate Google Maps into an address input field. However, I felt this didn't fit well with the client's existing stack, since they were already using Azure tools extensively across the project — Azure Search, Azure Blob Storage, and others. The client, though, was set on using Google Maps.
task: I needed to make the case for switching to Azure Maps instead, despite the client already having a clear preference for Google Maps, and back it up with more than just a gut feeling about stack consistency.
action: Instead of just pushing back verbally, I did research comparing the two options and found that Azure Maps would actually come out cheaper than Google Maps for our use case, on top of fitting better with the rest of the client's Azure-based infrastructure. I wrote up documentation laying out the research and presented it to the client.
result: After seeing the research, the client decided to switch to Azure Maps instead of insisting on their original choice. I implemented the Azure Maps integration myself, and it has been working properly in production with no complaints since.

situation: I was asked to create a Statement of Work (SOW) document for a client based only on meeting notes and a conversation with my manager. The client was an editing company that wanted a CMS to manage versions and comments. During the meeting where the SOW was discussed, I picked up that the client wasn't happy — they felt the price was too high, and they were actually hoping for something with more advanced AI integration rather than just a standard CMS.
task: I needed to respond to the client's concerns in real time, even though my role was to deliver the SOW, not necessarily to redesign the proposed solution on the spot.
action: Drawing on my background as a generalist — having worked as an editor, teacher, QA engineer, and full-stack engineer — I recognized that a traditional CMS with manual editing workflows didn't match what the client actually needed. I proposed an alternative: skip building a custom UI initially, and instead start with AI integration that could flag potential issues during proofreading, like an automated first-pass review.
result: The client responded positively over email, expressing real interest in the idea.

situation: We were working on a merchant onboarding application meant to be a single standard flow for an acquirer's merchants. The problem was that one-size-fits-all didn't really work — a small single-shop merchant had to go through the same onboarding process as a high-risk merchant like a casino. To address this, I was given the task of creating an onboarding flow that could be customized based on merchant risk level. The only direction I had was a very high-level, hand-drawn sketch from my team lead.
task: I needed to take that rough sketch and turn it into a working feature that let the onboarding flow and its questions be configured differently depending on risk level, with very little detailed specification to go on.
action: Based on the hand-drawn mockup, I built out the full CRUD functionality for the onboarding flow — the ability to create, read, update, and delete both the flow itself and its associated questions. After testing and shipping the initial version, I didn't stop there: I added further improvements on my own initiative, including drag-and-drop reordering for the flow steps and additional styling refinements to make it more usable.
result: The feature is currently working well in production with no complaints. It noticeably improved onboarding speed — merchants now move through the risk-based onboarding process much faster than before.

situation: On the frontend team, we relied on a third-party UI library for components. That library had a lot of complicated underlying code, and from time to time we'd wake up to find things broken on the frontend due to issues in that library — even though it had nothing to do with our own code. It was frustrating having to explain to clients that something was broken because of a dependency we didn't control, not because of our own work.
task: We needed a way to reduce our reliance on this fragile third-party library, especially for simple, frequently-used components, so that bugs in their code would stop becoming our problem.
action: I built a small internal component library for simple, common elements like tags and similar basic UI pieces, using our own styles instead of the third-party library's. We also set up a single source of truth for design through tokenization — shared values for fonts, colors, and other design tokens — so our styling stayed consistent and reusable across the app. For some elements, we didn't even need full custom components; we relied on simple global CSS, reserving custom components only for cases where that level of structure was actually needed.
result: This significantly reduced the number of UI bugs we ran into, since we were no longer exposed to the third-party library's issues for the components we'd replaced. The design tokenization also made our styling more consistent and easier to maintain across the app.

situation: At Intergalactic Agency, an external client wanted to track iPad app usage across their managed fleet, but the data only existed inside their Mosyle MDM admin dashboard — Mosyle didn't expose it through any public API. The client had been pulling this manually.
task: I needed to build a fully unattended pipeline that logged into Mosyle, pulled a rolling usage report, reshaped it into a custom 'which iPads used which apps' report, and delivered it to the client on a schedule — working against a real, unversioned admin UI instead of a stable API.
action: I built a Puppeteer script running in AWS Lambda on an EventBridge schedule every 3 days. It logs into Mosyle, navigates to DNS Filtering → Logs, sets a rolling 3-day range through the actual date-picker widget, and triggers an export; separately it navigates to the Reports page, grabs the exported file's download link, and fetches its CSV content directly using the authenticated session's cookies rather than wiring up headless Chromium's CDP download handling and polling a Lambda /tmp path. The reshaped report gets uploaded to S3 and emailed to the client as a link. Because Mosyle's UI is asynchronous, fields could exist in the DOM before they were interactive, so I leaned on page.waitForSelector() before every interaction plus a few explicit delay(5000) guards at the specific points that didn't expose a clean 'ready' signal — after the password field appears, after the start-date field appears, and after triggering the export. The custom calendar widget also needed date-specific JS logic to figure out whether the start day fell in the previous month, clicking a data-date attribute rather than typing into an input. I deliberately scoped this tightly to one site I could inspect and hardcode against rather than building something generic.
result: The automation has been running with no humans in the loop, replacing the client's manual process and earning strong client feedback. It's brittle to Mosyle changing their DOM, but I accepted that trade-off because it only targets one site checked every 3 days — if it breaks, the failure mode is just a missing report plus Lambda's own error logs, not a silent bad result, so no extra alerting was needed for that scope.

situation: At El Paso Labs, I worked on the crawl pipeline for a RAG dashboard that ingests arbitrary customer-configured websites into a search index. Some pages could be fetched cheaply; others needed a real browser to execute JavaScript before there was any content to read at all.
task: I needed to decide when it was actually worth paying for a full headless browser versus a plain HTTP fetch, since running headless browsers against an unbounded, growing set of customer domains is exactly the kind of automation that gets expensive fast if it isn't bounded.
action: I made a plain httpx request the default path — sitemap fetch, conditional HEAD with ETag/If-Modified-Since, then a SHA-256 content-hash check — and only fell back to a Playwright-based fetch when a plain GET came back empty, meaning the page needed JS execution to render. I capped that fallback at 5 concurrent instances per the pool's documented limit so it couldn't scale unbounded against arbitrary customer domains.
result: Most unchanged or static pages never touch the expensive browser path at all, and the concurrency cap keeps the fallback from becoming a runaway cost center as more customers get onboarded. I also identified a real limit in my own design: for JS-rendered sites that don't expose caching headers, Playwright still fires on every sync cycle since the hash check downstream only prevents a redundant re-upload, not a redundant render — something I'd tighten further given more time.

situation: At El Paso Labs, I worked on the crawl pipeline that feeds an AI agent's knowledge of the web for a RAG dashboard — it crawls arbitrary customer-configured websites, converts pages to clean Markdown, and keeps an Azure AI Search index in sync with what's actually live on those sites, so the agent's answers are grounded in current content instead of stale or hallucinated information.
task: Beyond just fetching pages, I needed the crawler to behave like a good citizen on the web rather than a blunt scraper, and to keep the index itself trustworthy as source pages changed or disappeared — all while staying affordable to run continuously across many customer domains.
action: I built the crawler to fetch and respect robots.txt before issuing a single request — a RobotsPolicy that can outright block a source, plus a Crawl-delay directive that throttles every subsequent request. I also had it explicitly fetch llms.txt, the emerging convention where sites publish a curated, LLM-friendly version of their content, and prioritized those URLs over anything discovered through sitemap or crawling, since that's the site telling AI agents 'read this, it's the clean version.' For index trustworthiness, pages that 404/410 get deleted from the index immediately, and a separate cleanup pass catches pages that silently vanished from a sitemap without ever 404ing. To keep it affordable, most of the pipeline never touches a real browser — HTTP conditional requests and a content hash decide whether a page even needs re-processing — and real rendering with Playwright only kicks in when a page needs JS to produce content at all, pool-capped so it can't take the service down under unpredictable load.
result: The agent's answers stay grounded in what's actually live on customer sites rather than stale or deleted content, the crawler doesn't hammer or get blocked by the sites it visits, and the expensive rendering path stays bounded instead of scaling unpredictably with the number of customer domains.

situation: While building and testing the El Paso Labs agent that reads incoming emails and decides whether to create a task in Airtable, I found a real failure mode: the model wasn't just getting fields wrong sometimes — it was occasionally inventing values with full confidence, like attaching a due date to an email that never mentioned one, or filling in an assignee when no owner was ever indicated. A hallucinated due date looks exactly like a real one to anyone downstream, so this could easily have shipped unnoticed.
task: I needed to make sure this specific failure mode was actually caught and fixed before shipping, rather than trusting that a handful of manual spot-checks and a quick prompt tweak would reliably catch a failure mode that looks exactly as confident and well-formatted as a correct answer.
action: Instead of shipping on manual testing, I built an offline evaluation pipeline — a repeatable test harness that runs the model against a labeled set of real examples instead of relying on someone remembering to eyeball it. Critically, I didn't just add 'does the output match' accuracy checks — for every example where the correct answer for a field was genuinely nothing, the pipeline explicitly scores whether the model invented a value anyway. That's a deliberate, separate check from plain accuracy, since accuracy alone only measures cases where a real answer exists and says nothing about the model fabricating one when the right answer was silence.
result: The eval pipeline caught the hallucination failure mode systematically rather than relying on luck or manual review, and became part of how we detected LLM regressions before every production deployment going forward — turning a failure I stumbled on in testing into a permanent safeguard.

situation: I was working on a project for an editing and publishing client. The original request, passed to me secondhand from an earlier conversation, was for a big build: a full marketplace where outside organizations could browse and license content, plus a custom-built tool for managing submissions.
task: There was no PM on this — I needed to figure out what to actually build myself, and decide what to cut from a large, already-agreed-upon vision without anyone else forcing that call.
action: Instead of building what had been asked for secondhand, I sat in on a meeting and heard the real problem directly from the person who dealt with it every day. Having worked as an editor myself in a past life, I recognized his actual pain immediately: he was constantly chasing people for missing submission pieces, reading everything from scratch with no help, and had no visibility into what stage anything was at — none of which required a marketplace to fix. I wrote directly to the client myself proposing we start with something simple and ready-made instead of a custom tool, and put our real energy into an assistant that helps him review incoming submissions. I used an existing, off-the-shelf admin system as-is for the first version rather than designing new interfaces from scratch, pushed the marketplace itself to a later phase, explicitly marked notifications, advanced permissions, and multi-org support as not happening yet instead of quietly dropping them, and cut the fancier AI add-ons (auto-summaries, captions, translations, draft emails) until the one core feature proved it worked. I also deliberately avoided a complex multi-step AI framework for the review assistant — one simple request was enough — and wrote that decision down so it could be revisited later. Later, I tightened scope again, telling the client the very first version was a free trial meant only to answer one question: is this the right foundation to build on, with the AI assistant and marketplace explicitly held back as separate paid phases agreed on in advance.
result: The client got a version that solved the actual, felt problem quickly instead of waiting on a much larger build, and everything cut was written down in plain language so scope only grew back deliberately later, never by accident. Without anyone else forcing a cut, I found the smallest piece that solved the real problem rather than defaulting to building the entire original vision at once.
